case_info.scenario: A 37-year-old woman with a history of resolved nasopharyngeal carcinoma presented with transient binocular horizontal diplopia for 2 years. She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

She received chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, along with radiotherapy (70 Gy in 33 fractions), which was completed 9 years earlier. Seven years later, she developed intermittent horizontal diplopia when she looked into an eccentric lateral gaze. She felt cramps around her eye and dizziness with the diplopia. When she experienced diplopia, she closed her eyes for rest for approximately 2 minutes, after which the diplopia improved. She denied any history of ptosis, weakness, or dysarthria. She had no other medical history or current medications. Physical examination revealed a resting eye position in the midline and a full range of motion in horizontal movements (Figure, A). Following a prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute, she developed involuntary contraction of the right lateral rectus, which resulted in right exotropia (Figure, B andVideo, A). The movements of the other extraocular muscles showed a full range of motion, with no nystagmus or involuntary contractions similar to those of the right lateral rectus muscle. Other neurological examinations revealed tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle. Laboratory investigations revealed normal thyroid function test results, and the patient was negative for acetylcholine receptor antibody and muscle-specific kinase antibody. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and cranial nerves demonstrated no recurrence of nasopharyngeal carcinoma and no vascular compression of the abducens nerve.

Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact

- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

case_info.caption: A, Extraocular muscle examination at resting eye position. B, Exotropia of the right eye after prolonged eccentric gaze to the right for approximately 1 minute.
case_info.explanation: This patient’s clinical presentation, characterized by recurrent episodes of transient diplopia and strabismus, intermittent exotropia after prolonged eccentric gaze, and a history of postradiation therapy and signs of postradiation sequelae, including tongue atrophy with fasciculations and myokymia in the trapezius muscle, suggests a diagnosis of ocular neuromyotonia (ONM) due to postradiation cranial neuropathy. Her diplopia pattern, developing spontaneously or after prolonged eccentric gaze, is consistent with ONM. The treatment of choice is carbamazepine, which is appropriate for this condition (option B). Option A is incorrect, as pyridostigmine is typically preferred for patients with myasthenia gravis, which can present with ophthalmoplegia similar to this patient’s symptoms. However, the patient’s clinical presentation and negative acetylcholine receptor antibody findings do not support this diagnosis. Strabismus surgery (option C) is not beneficial for patients with ONM and in some cases may exacerbate episodes of ONM. Reevaluation with MRI of the brain and orbit (option D) could be beneficial for patients experiencing progressively worsening ocular motor or other neurological abnormalities to assess for potential disease recurrence. Ocular neuromyotonia is an episodic, involuntary, sustained contraction of 1 or more extraocular muscles that causes patients to develop intermittent diplopia, often triggered by sustained gaze in the direction of these muscles’ action.1The pathogenesis of ONM is hypothesized to arise from focal demyelination of cranial nerves that supply the extraocular muscles, resulting in ephaptic transmission of damaged fibers. An assumption of axonal hyperexcitability and ephaptic neural transmission is the underlying mechanism causative of the episodic extraocular muscle contractions of ONM.2,3 ONM is a rare condition. A retrospective study using the Mayo Clinic electronic medical record system, conducted from January 2004 to January 2023, identified 42 cases.2The most common etiology of ONM is a history of radiation, accounting for more than 90% of cases, particularly following radiation targeting the sellar, parasellar, and skull base regions. The median radiation dose is 50 Gy (range, 12.5-76 Gy).2Other reported causes include thyroid-related orbitopathy, stroke, head trauma, supraclinoid aneurysm, demyelinating diseases, and prior strabismus surgery.1,2,4Idiopathic ONM is believed to be caused by vascular compression, similar to the proposed mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia or hemifacial spasm.5The most commonly affected cranial nerve in ONM is the abducens nerve (74%), followed by the oculomotor nerve (45%) and the trochlear nerve (7%).2The onset of ONM typically occurs approximately 9 years after radiation. Most patients with ONM are misdiagnosed with ocular myasthenia gravis, dry eye, tumor progression, or vestibular disease.2 Treatment recommendations for ONM include avoiding eccentric gazes that trigger episodes. Antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, are also recommended to reduce the symptoms of ONM.2,6,7Spontaneous resolution is rare. Most patients (95%) experience improvement or resolution of symptoms after starting medication.2Strabismus surgery is not advantageous for patients with ONM and in some instances may worsen ONM episodes.2,4 The patient’s manifestations of ONM were managed by her multidisciplinary health care team. She was treated with 200 mg of carbamazepine after confirming a negative result of the HLA-B*1502 test, which is used to predict the risk of carbamazepine-induced allergic reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Three months after starting medication, her diplopia symptoms resolved with no presentation of diplopia after prolonged eccentric gaze (Video, B). Long-term treatment with carbamazepine and follow-up every 3 months to assess symptoms, complete blood cell count, and serum sodium level to monitor for potential adverse effects of carbamazepine were recommended.
